content.short_questions:
What is a cell?

    Answer: A cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of a living organism, capable of carrying out essential life
    processes.

 What is a selectively permeable membrane?

    Answer: A selectively permeable membrane allows some substances to pass through while restricting others.
content.long_questions:
Describe the structure and functions of the plasma membrane.

    Answer: The plasma membrane is a thin, flexible boundary made mainly of a phospholipid bilayer with embedded
    proteins, cholesterol and carbohydrate chains. Hydrophilic heads face the watery environments and hydrophobic tails
    face inward. It separates the cell from its surroundings, controls movement of substances, receives signals, supports
    cell recognition and helps maintain homeostasis.

 • DNA stores hereditary information; genes are functional sequences of DNA.

chapters.title: Cell Division

content.overview:
Cell division produces new cells for growth, repair and reproduction. Mitosis usually produces two genetically similar
 daughter cells, whereas meiosis reduces chromosome number and produces genetically varied cells for sexual
 reproduction.
key_terms: Interphase includes G1, S and G2; DNA is replicated during S phase.
Mitosis proceeds through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis.
Meiosis consists of two divisions after one DNA replication; homologous chromosomes pair in prophase I.
Crossing over and independent assortment contribute to genetic variation.
study_notes: Interphase includes G1, S and G2; DNA is replicated during S phase.
Mitosis proceeds through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis.
Meiosis consists of two divisions after one DNA replication; homologous chromosomes pair in prophase I.
Crossing over and independent assortment contribute to genetic variation.
Uncontrolled cell-cycle regulation can contribute to tumour formation.
content.short_questions:
What is mitosis?

    Answer: Mitosis is nuclear division that normally produces two daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number as
    the parent nucleus.

 What is crossing over?

    Answer: Crossing over is the exchange of corresponding DNA segments between non-sister chromatids of
    homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
content.long_questions:
Differentiate between mitosis and meiosis.

    Answer: Mitosis involves one nuclear division and normally produces two genetically similar cells with the same
    chromosome number as the parent. It supports growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Meiosis involves two
    successive divisions after one DNA replication and normally produces four haploid cells. Homologous pairing, crossing
    over and independent assortment occur in meiosis, creating variation and reducing chromosome number for sexual
    reproduction.

mcqs.content: What type of cell division occurs in bacteria, blue-green algae, and amoeba without spindle formation? A. Mitosis B. Amitosis (direct cell division) C. Meiosis D. Multiple fission Answer: B
In the eukaryotic cell cycle, during which phase of interphase does DNA replication occur? A. G1 phase B. S phase (Synthesis phase) C. G2 phase D. M phase Answer: B

What is the correct chronological sequence of stages in mitosis? A. Metaphase -> Anaphase -> Prophase -> Telophase B. Prophase -> Prometaphase -> Metaphase -> Anaphase -> Telophase C. Anaphase -> Metaphase -> Telophase -> Prophase D. Interphase -> Cytokinesis Answer: B
During which stage of mitosis do chromosomes align along the equatorial (metaphase) plate? A. Prophase B. Metaphase C. Anaphase D. Telophase Answer: B

During which stage of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles as daughter chromosomes? A. Metaphase B. Anaphase (forming V, L, J, I shapes based on centromere position) C. Telophase D. Prophase Answer: B
What are metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, and telocentric chromosomes' respective shapes during anaphase? A. L, V, I, J B. V, L, J, and I C. I, J, V, L D. V, V, L, L Answer: B

Cytokinesis in plant cells occurs primarily by the formation of a: A. Cleavage furrow from outside B. Cell plate progressing centrifugally from center by phragmoplast vesicles C. Contractile ring D. Budding Answer: B

Meiosis is termed 'reduction division' because in Meiosis I: A. Chromosome number doubles B. Chromosome number is halved from diploid (2n) to haploid (n) C. Chromatids do not separate D. DNA content remains 4C Answer: B

What are the five substages of Prophase I of Meiosis in order? A. Pachytene -> Zygotene -> Leptotene -> Diplotene -> Diakinesis B. Leptotene -> Zygotene -> Pachytene -> Diplotene -> Diakinesis C. Zygotene -> Pachytene -> Diplotene -> Diakinesis -> Leptotene D. Diplotene -> Diakinesis -> Leptotene -> Zygotene -> Pachytene Answer: B
During which substage of Prophase I does synapsis (pairing of homologous chromosomes to form bivalents) occur? A. Leptotene B. Zygotene C. Pachytene D. Diplotene Answer: B

During which substage of Prophase I does crossing over and chiasma formation occur between non-sister chromatids? A. Zygotene B. Pachytene (with enzyme recombinase) C. Diplotene D. Diakinesis Answer: B

What is the evolutionary significance of crossing over during meiosis? A. Maintains identical clones B. Creates genetic recombination and variation in offspring C. Prevents mutations D. Reduces chromosome size Answer: B
During which substage of Prophase I do homologous chromosomes begin to repel each other, leaving X-shaped chiasmata clearly visible? A. Zygotene B. Diplotene C. Pachytene D. Diakinesis Answer: B
Terminalization of chiasmata is completed in which substage of Prophase I? A. Pachytene B. Diakinesis C. Diplotene D. Leptotene Answer: B

Meiosis II is equational division similar to mitosis because: A. Chromosome number is halved again B. Sister chromatids separate, maintaining haploid chromosome number n in all 4 daughter cells C. DNA replicates D. Crossing over recurs Answer: B
How many haploid daughter cells are produced from one diploid parent cell at the end of complete meiosis? A. 2 B. 4 C. 8 D. 1 Answer: B
Uncontrolled, unregulated mitotic cell division leads to the formation of: A. Benign scar B. Malignant tumor / Cancer C. Normal callus D. Haploid tissue Answer: B
What protein kinase complexes regulate progression through cell cycle checkpoints (G1/S and G2/M)? A. Catalase B. Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) and Cyclins C. Amylase D. Polymerase Answer: B
What is programmed cell death (physiological cell suicide) called in multicellular organisms? A. Necrosis B. Apoptosis C. Autophagy D. Lysis Answer: B
In humans (2n = 46), how many chromosomes are present in a secondary spermatocyte or oocyte after Meiosis I? A. 46 B. 23 (each with 2 sister chromatids) C. 92 D. 12 Answer: B

content.short_questions:
What is an enzyme?

    Answer: An enzyme is a biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up a chemical reaction without being
    consumed.

 What is a peptide bond?

    Answer: A peptide bond is the covalent bond that links the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amino group of

content.long_questions:
Explain the factors that affect enzyme activity.

    Answer: Enzyme activity depends on temperature, pH, substrate concentration and enzyme concentration. Activity
    generally rises with temperature to an optimum, after which denaturation reduces activity. Each enzyme has an
    optimum pH. Increasing substrate concentration raises the rate until active sites become saturated. Inhibitors may
    reduce activity by binding to the active site or another site.

mcqs.content: What is the general empirical formula for most carbohydrates (hydrates of carbon)? A. Cn(H2O)n or (CH2O)n B. CnH2nO2 C. CnHnOn D. C2nHnOn Answer: A

What is the principal energy storage polysaccharide in animals and fungi, stored in liver and muscle? A. Cellulose B. Glycogen ('animal starch') C. Starch D. Inulin Answer: B
What are the basic monomeric building blocks of proteins? A. Fatty acids B. Amino acids (20 standard proteinogenic alpha-amino acids) C. Nucleotides D. Monosaccharides Answer: B
What covalent bond joins two amino acids with the elimination of a water molecule? A. Glycosidic bond B. Peptide bond (-CO-NH-) C. Phosphodiester bond D. Ester bond Answer: B
Which secondary structure of proteins is stabilized by intrachain hydrogen bonds (e.g. In alpha-keratin)? A. Beta-pleated sheet B. Alpha-helix C. Disulfide bridge D. Hydrophobic core Answer: B
Hemoglobin is an example of what level of protein structural organization? A. Primary B. Quaternary structure (four polypeptide subunits: 2 alpha + 2 beta) C. Secondary D. Tertiary only Answer: B

What is the lock-and-key model of enzyme action proposed by Emil Fischer in 1894? A. Enzyme changes shape permanently B. Substrate fits precisely into the complementary active site of the enzyme like a key in a lock C. Enzyme is consumed D. All enzymes act everywhere Answer: B

The non-protein organic molecule tightly or loosely bound to an enzyme required for its catalytic activity is called a: A. Apoenzyme B. Coenzyme / Cofactor / Prosthetic group C. Zymogen D. Inhibitor Answer: B
What is a complete, catalytically active enzyme consisting of an apoenzyme plus its cofactor called? A. Coenzyme B. Holoenzyme (Apoenzyme + Cofactor = Holoenzyme) C. Proenzyme D. Ribozyme Answer: B
What are biological RNA molecules that possess catalytic enzymatic activity called? A. Apoenzymes B. Ribozymes C. Isozymes D. Abzymes Answer: B

A triglyceride (neutral fat) is an ester formed from: A. One glycerol and one fatty acid B. One glycerol molecule and three fatty acid molecules C. Three glycerols and one fatty acid D. Fatty acid and alcohol only Answer: B

What is the difference between saturated and unsaturated fatty acids? A. Saturated have double bonds B. Saturated have only single C-C bonds; unsaturated contain one or more C=C double bonds C. Unsaturated are solids at room temperature D. Saturated are essential Answer: B
What is the monomeric repeating unit of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA)? A. Nucleoside B. Nucleotide (Nitrogenous base + Pentose sugar + Phosphate group) C. Amino acid D. Purine only Answer: B
Which nitrogenous base is present in RNA but absent in DNA? A. Thymine B. Uracil (replaces thymine) C. Cytosine D. Adenine Answer: B

According to Chargaff's rule in double-stranded DNA, what is the base-pairing ratio? A. A = C and G = T B. A = T and G = C (Purines = Pyrimidines: A + G = T + C) C. A + T = G + C D. A = G = C = T Answer: B

chapters.title: Microorganisms

content.overview:
Microorganisms include viruses, bacteria, protozoa and microscopic fungi. They influence health, ecosystems, food
 production and industry. Some cause disease, while others recycle nutrients or are useful in biotechnology.
key_terms: Viruses are acellular and replicate only inside suitable host cells.
Bacteria are prokaryotes; their DNA is not enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus.
Bacteria may reproduce by binary fission and exchange genes through mechanisms such as conjugation.
Protozoa are eukaryotic; Plasmodium causes malaria and is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes.
study_notes: Viruses are acellular and replicate only inside suitable host cells.
Bacteria are prokaryotes; their DNA is not enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus.
Bacteria may reproduce by binary fission and exchange genes through mechanisms such as conjugation.
Protozoa are eukaryotic; Plasmodium causes malaria and is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes.
Microorganisms are used in fermentation, medicine, agriculture and waste treatment.
content.short_questions:
Why are viruses called obligate intracellular parasites?

    Answer: They can reproduce only inside living host cells because they depend on host-cell machinery.

 What causes malaria?

    Answer: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium species, which are transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected
    female Anopheles mosquito.
content.long_questions:
Describe the main differences between bacteria and viruses.

    Answer: Bacteria are living prokaryotic cells with cellular organisation, cytoplasm, ribosomes and genetic material;
    many reproduce independently by binary fission. Viruses are acellular particles containing DNA or RNA within a protein
    coat, sometimes with an envelope. They lack their own metabolism and ribosomes and replicate only inside host cells.
    Antibiotics may act against susceptible bacteria but do not treat viral infections.

mcqs.content: Are viruses classified as living cellular organisms or non-cellular infectious biological entities? A. Prokaryotic cells B. Non-cellular obligate intracellular parasites consisting of nucleic acid inside a protein capsid C. Eukaryotic cells D. Fungi Answer: B
What type of nucleic acid is present in Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV)? A. Double-stranded DNA B. Single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) C. Double-stranded RNA D. Both DNA and RNA Answer: B
What is the complete, infectious viral particle outside a host cell called? A. Capsomere B. Virion C. Viroid D. Prion Answer: B
What infectious agents consist solely of misfolded protein with no nucleic acid (e.g. Causing Mad Cow Disease)? A. Viroids B. Prions C. Virions D. Bacteriophages Answer: B
What are infectious plant pathogens consisting only of short, circular single-stranded RNA without protein coat? A. Prions B. Viroids C. Virions D. Bacteriophages Answer: B

What type of virus is T2 or T4 bacteriophage that infects Escherichia coli bacteria? A. RNA enveloped virus B. DNA virus with icosahedral head, collar, and contractile tail with tail fibers C. Plant virus D. Retrovirus Answer: B

In the lytic cycle of a virulent bacteriophage, what is the fate of the host bacterial cell? A. Survives indefinitely B. Lyses and bursts, releasing hundreds of new virions C. Integrates viral genome safely D. Becomes spore Answer: B
In the lysogenic cycle (e.g. Lambda phage), what is the viral genome integrated into the bacterial chromosome called? A. Virion B. Prophage (or provirus) C. Capsid D. Plasmagene Answer: B
Which human disease is caused by Dengue virus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes? A. Malaria B. Dengue hemorrhagic fever (caused by Flavivirus ssRNA) C. Typhoid D. Kala-azar Answer: B

What is the primary genetic material and reverse transcriptase enzyme system of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)? A. dsDNA B. Single-stranded RNA (Retrovirus) producing DNA copy via reverse transcriptase C. dsRNA D. Bacterial plasmid Answer: B
What is the primary chemical component of bacterial cell walls that is stained in Gram staining? A. Cellulose B. Peptidoglycan (murein composed of NAG and NAM chains) C. Chitin D. Silica Answer: B

In Gram staining (Crystal violet, Iodine, Alcohol, Safranin), Gram-positive bacteria appear: A. Pink/Red B. Purple / Violet (thick peptidoglycan retains crystal violet-iodine complex) C. Colorless D. Green Answer: B
What is the small, circular, self-replicating extrachromosomal DNA molecule found in many bacteria called? A. Chromosome B. Plasmid C. Mesosome D. Nucleoid Answer: B
What bacterial appendage is used for attachment and bacterial conjugation (transfer of genetic material)? A. Flagellum B. Pilus (sex pilus / fimbriae) C. Capsule D. Mesosome Answer: B

Which bacterium causes cholera in humans via contaminated water and rice-water stool? A. Salmonella typhi B. Vibrio cholerae (comma-shaped Gram-negative bacterium) C. Mycobacterium tuberculosis D. Bacillus anthracis Answer: B
Which bacterium causes tuberculosis in humans? A. Corynebacterium diphtheriae B. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast bacillus) C. Streptococcus pneumoniae D. Clostridium tetani Answer: B
Which genus of protozoan parasite causes Malaria in humans? A. Entamoeba B. Plasmodium (e.g., P. vivax, P. falciparum) C. Leishmania D. Trypanosoma Answer: B

What is the vector that transmits Plasmodium malaria parasites to humans? A. Male Anopheles mosquito B. Female Anopheles mosquito (takes blood meal for egg development) C. Culex mosquito D. Aedes aegypti Answer: B

In which human organ and blood cell do Plasmodium parasites undergo schizogony and multiplication? A. Lungs and WBCs B. Liver parenchymal cells (hepatic schizogony) and Red Blood Cells (erythrocytic schizogony) C. Kidney D. Brain Answer: B

What toxic substance released upon the rupture of infected red blood cells causes periodic fever and chills in malaria? A. Bilirubin B. Hemozoin (malarial pigment) and pyrogens C. Urea D. Histamine Answer: B

Why are bryophytes called amphibians of the plant kingdom?

 What is a sorus?

They grow on terrestrial soil but require external water for flagellated sperm to swim to the archegonium for fertilization C. They have vascular tissues D. They bear flowers in water Answer: B
In the life cycle of bryophytes, which generation is the dominant, independent, photosynthetic phase? A. Sporophyte (2n) B. Gametophyte (haploid, n) C. Zygote D. Capsule Answer: B

Do Bryophytes possess true roots, stems, leaves, or vascular bundles (xylem and phloem)? A. Yes, well-developed B. No, they lack true vascular bundles and have root-like rhizoids C. Only xylem is present D. They have woody stems Answer: B

In Riccia, what is the nature and morphological structure of the gametophytic plant body? A. Cylindrical stem B. Dichotomously branched, dorsiventrally flattened green thallus C. Tree-like D. Filamentous only Answer: B
Where are the sporophytes of Riccia embedded? A. On aerial stalks B. Embedded completely inside the gametophytic thallus tissue C. On leaves D. Outside water Answer: B

Pteridophytes (ferns) are distinct from Bryophytes because Pteridophytes are: A. Non-vascular B. Vascular cryptogams (possessing xylem and phloem, dominant sporophyte 2n) C. Seed-bearing D. Flowering plants Answer: B

What are the large, compound leaves of ferns called? A. Microphylls B. Fronds C. Scales D. Bracts Answer: B
What is the coiled, circinate vernation of young immature fern fronds called? A. Tendril B. Circinate vernation (crozier / fiddlehead) C. Budding D. Venation Answer: B
What are the clusters of sporangia found on the underside of fertile fern leaflets called? A. Cones B. Sori (singular: Sorus, often covered by indusium) C. Strobilus D. Capsules Answer: B
What specialized ring of thickened cells on a fern sporangium hygroscopically tears it open to disperse spores? A. Lip cells B. Annulus (and stomium) C. Operculum D. Peristome Answer: B

What is the heart-shaped, photosynthetic, independent haploid gametophyte of a fern called? A. Thallus B. Prothallus (bearing antheridia on posterior rhizoid region and archegonia near apical notch) C. Protonema D. Rhizome Answer: B

What is heterospory in Pteridophytes (e.g. Selaginella)? A. Production of one spore type B. Production of two distinct spore types: microspores (male) and megaspores (female), representing precursor to seed habit C. Asexual spores only D. Seed production Answer: B

Which Pteridophyte is commonly known as 'horsetail' and has silica-rich abrasive ribbed stems? A. Lycopodium B. Equisetum C. Selaginella D. Isoetes Answer: B
In mosses (Funaria), what is the juvenile, filamentous green stage that develops from spore germination called? A. Prothallus B. Protonema C. Rhizoid D. Operculum Answer: B
What is the calyptra in a moss sporophyte? A. Spore mass B. Protective cap over the capsule derived from the archegonial wall (gametophytic tissue) C. Basal foot D. Peristome tooth Answer: B

What is double fertilisation?

What family of Angiosperms includes rice, wheat, corn, bamboo, and sugarcane? A. Fabaceae B. Poaceae (Gramineae, the Grass family) C. Malvaceae D. Solanaceae Answer: B

 tissues perform functions such as protection, support, storage and transport.

Sclerenchyma has thick, often lignified walls and provides mechanical strength.

content.short_questions:
What is meristematic tissue?

    Answer: Meristematic tissue consists of actively dividing, relatively undifferentiated plant cells responsible for growth.

 What is the main function of xylem?

    Answer: Xylem conducts water and dissolved mineral ions from roots to other parts and also provides support.
content.long_questions:
Describe the three major plant tissue systems.

    Answer: The epidermal tissue system forms the outer protective covering and may include stomata and root hairs.
    The ground tissue system includes tissues involved in photosynthesis, storage and support. The vascular tissue
    system consists of xylem and phloem: xylem transports water and minerals, while phloem transports sugars and other
    organic substances.

What are the four constituent cellular elements of complex Phloem vascular tissue in Angiosperms? A. Tracheids and vessels B. Sieve tube elements, Companion cells, Phloem parenchyma, and Phloem fibers (bast fibers) C. Tracheids and sieve cells D. Xylem fibers Answer: B

Which living conducting element of phloem lacks a nucleus at functional maturity but is metabolically assisted by a nucleated companion cell? A. Phloem parenchyma B. Sieve tube element C. Bast fiber D. Vessel Answer: B
A vascular bundle containing both xylem and phloem on the same radius is termed: A. Radial B. Conjoint (collateral or bicollateral) C. Concentric D. Exarch Answer: B

A collateral vascular bundle possessing active vascular cambium between xylem and phloem capable of secondary growth is: A. Closed bundle B. Open vascular bundle (characteristic of dicot stems) C. Radial bundle D. Concentric bundle Answer: B

In primary roots of both dicots and monocots, how are xylem and phloem strands arranged? A. Conjoint collateral B. Radial (arranged along alternating radii separated by parenchymatous conjunctive tissue) C. Concentric D. Bicollateral Answer: B
What is the outermost waxy, water-impermeable protective layer deposited by the epidermal cells called? A. Suberin B. Cuticle (composed of cutin) C. Lignin D. Pectin Answer: B

What specialized kidney-shaped (in dicots) or dumbbell-shaped (in monocots) cells flank each stomatal pore to regulate transpiration? A. Subsidiary cells B. Guard cells (possessing chloroplasts) C. Trichomes D. Bulliform cells Answer: B

What is transpiration?

Explain the light-dependent and light-independent stages of photosynthesis.

    Answer: The light-dependent reactions occur in thylakoid membranes. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, water is split,

According to Levitt's active K+ transport theory, stomata open in daylight due to: A. Efflux of potassium ions B. Active influx of K+ ions and malate into guard cells, lowering osmotic potential and causing endosmosis of water C. Closing of pore D. Loss of turgor pressure Answer: B

The exudation of liquid water droplets from hydathodes at leaf margins under high root pressure and humidity is called: A. Transpiration B. Guttation C. Bleeding D. Evaporation Answer: B

What drives the long-distance upward movement of water in tall trees against gravity according to Dixon and Joly (1894)? A. Capillarity only B. Cohesion-Tension-Transpiration Pull mechanism C. Root pressure alone D. Active transport in phloem Answer: B

In the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis, what process splits water molecules (photolysis) to release O2 and electrons? A. Calvin cycle B. Photolysis of water at Oxygen-Evolving Complex (OEC) of Photosystem II (PS II) C. Cyclic photophosphorylation D. Rubisco activity Answer: B
What are the two assimilatory powers generated during light reactions used to drive CO2 fixation in stroma? A. ADP and NADP+ B. ATP and NADPH + H+ C. Glucose and O2 D. Pyruvate and FADH2 Answer: B

What is the primary CO2 acceptor and the first stable 3-carbon product in the Calvin cycle (C3 pathway)? A. PEP and Oxaloacetate B. Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP) and 3-Phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA) C. Pyruvate and Glucose D. OAA and Malate Answer: B

What key enzyme catalyzes the carboxylation of RuBP in C3 plants (the most abundant protein on Earth)? A. PEP carboxylase B. RuBisCO (Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase) C. Carbonic anhydrase D. ATP synthase Answer: B

In C4 plants (e.g. Corn, sugarcane, Amaranthus), what is the first stable 4-carbon product of CO2 fixation? A. 3-PGA B. Oxaloacetic acid (OAA, catalyzed by PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells) C. Malate D. Aspartate Answer: B

What specialized leaf anatomy with prominent chloroplast-rich bundle sheath cells is characteristic of C4 plants? A. Bifacial anatomy B. Kranz anatomy (wreath-like arrangement of bundle sheath cells) C. Isobilateral D. Dorsiventral Answer: B

What is the energetic advantage of C4 plants over C3 plants under high temperature and bright sunlight? A. They consume less ATP B. They suppress wasteful photorespiration by concentrating CO2 around RuBisCO in bundle sheath cells C. They don't need light D. They don't need water Answer: B

Glycolysis (EMP pathway), the universal first stage of cellular respiration, occurs in which cellular compartment? A. Mitochondrial matrix B. Cytosol / Cytoplasm (independent of oxygen) C. Inner mitochondrial membrane D. Chloroplast stroma Answer: B
What is the net yield of ATP and NADH per molecule of glucose oxidized in glycolysis? A. 4 ATP, 0 NADH B. 2 ATP (net) and 2 NADH + 2 H+ C. 36 ATP D. 1 ATP Answer: B
The Krebs cycle (Citric Acid Cycle / TCA cycle) occurs in which part of the eukaryotic cell? A. Cytoplasm B. Mitochondrial matrix C. Peroxisome D. Thylakoid lumen Answer: B
What is the 2-carbon compound that enters the Krebs cycle by condensing with 4-carbon oxaloacetate (OAA) to form citrate? A. Pyruvate B. Acetyl-CoA C. Lactate D. Ethanol Answer: B

In aerobic respiration, where is the Electron Transport Chain (ETC) and ATP synthase located? A. Outer mitochondrial membrane B. Inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae) C. Mitochondrial matrix D. Cytosol Answer: B
In anaerobic alcohol fermentation by yeast, pyruvate is decarboxylated and reduced to: A. Lactic acid B. Ethanol and Carbon dioxide (CO2) C. Acetic acid D. Methanol Answer: B

What is pollination?

    Answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma of a flower.

 What is vegetative propagation?

    Answer: Vegetative propagation is a form of asexual reproduction in which new plants develop from vegetative parts
    such as stems, roots or leaves.
content.long_questions:
Describe the sequence of sexual reproduction in a flowering plant.

    Answer: The flower produces pollen in the anther and an embryo sac in the ovule. Pollination transfers pollen to the
    stigma. A compatible pollen grain germinates and forms a pollen tube through the style. The male gametes reach the
    embryo sac and double fertilisation occurs. The zygote develops into an embryo, the ovule becomes a seed and the
    ovary usually develops into a fruit.

mcqs.content: What is the female reproductive unit (megasporophyll) of a flower called? A. Stamen B. Carpel / Pistil (consisting of stigma, style, and ovary) C. Sepal D. Petal Answer: B
What is the male reproductive unit (microsporophyll) of a flower called? A. Carpel B. Stamen (consisting of filament and pollen-bearing anther) C. Receptacle D. Pedicel Answer: B

What is microsporogenesis in angiosperms? A. Egg development B. The formation of haploid microspores (pollen grains) from a diploid microspore mother cell through meiosis C. Seed germination D. Fruit ripening Answer: B

At what stage of cellular maturity is an angiosperm pollen grain typically shed from the anther? A. 1-celled B. 2-celled (generative cell and vegetative/tube cell) or 3-celled (two sperm cells) C. 4-celled D. 8-celled Answer: B

A typical mature angiosperm female gametophyte (embryo sac, Polygonum type) consists of: A. 4 cells and 4 nuclei B. 7 cells and 8 nuclei (3 antipodal cells, 2 synergids, 1 egg cell, and 1 large central cell with 2 polar nuclei) C. 8 cells and 8 nuclei D. 1 egg only Answer: B
What is pollination defined as in botany? A. Fertilization B. The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the receptive stigma of a flower C. Seed dispersal D. Pollen germination Answer: B

What type of pollination occurs when pollen is transferred between flowers on the same plant or within the same bisexual flower? A. Xenogamy B. Self-pollination (Autogamy or Geitonogamy) C. Cross-pollination D. Hybridization Answer: B

Wind-pollinated (anemophilous) flowers are typically characterized by: A. Large bright fragrant petals with nectar B. Inconspicuous, non-fragrant flowers, light non-sticky pollen, and large feathery stigmas (e.g. Grasses, corn) C. Sticky nectar glands D. Heavy spiny pollen Answer: B

Insect-pollinated (entomophilous) flowers typically possess: A. Feathery stigmas and dull color B. Brightly colored petals, fragrant scent, and sugary nectar to attract insect pollinators C. Pollen released in water D. No petals Answer: B
What structure directs the pollen tube safely into the embryo sac through the micropylar opening? A. Antipodal cells B. Filiform apparatus of the synergid cells C. Nucellus D. Integuments Answer: B

In angiosperm double fertilization, what are the two separate fusion events? A. Two sperms fuse with one egg B. Sperm 1 (n) + Egg (n) -> 2n Zygote; Sperm 2 (n) + 2 Polar nuclei (2n) -> 3n Primary Endosperm Nucleus (PEN) C. Sperm fuses with antipodal cells D. Pollen fuses with stigma Answer: B
What does the ovule develop into after successful fertilization? A. Fruit B. Seed (with seed coat developed from integuments) C. Endosperm only D. Embryo sac Answer: B
What does the ovary wall develop into in a true fruit? A. Seed coat B. Pericarp (epicarp, mesocarp, and endocarp) C. Endosperm D. Thalamus Answer: B

What is parthenocarpy in plants? A. Development of seed without fertilization B. The development and formation of fruit without fertilization, resulting in seedless fruits (e.g. Banana, seedless grapes) C. Formation of twin embryos D. Flower dropping Answer: B

What is apomixis in angiosperms? A. Normal sexual reproduction B. The asexual production of seeds without fertilization or meiosis (mimicking sexual reproduction) C. Tissue culture D. Stem cutting Answer: B
What is the development of an embryo directly from an unfertilized egg cell called? A. Parthenocarpy B. Parthenogenesis C. Polymbryony D. Amphimixis Answer: B
What is the occurrence of more than one embryo in a single seed called (common in Citrus and mango)? A. Polyploidy B. Polyembryony C. Polyspermy D. Parthenocarpy Answer: B
In a fertilized seed, what embryonic structure develops into the primary root system? A. Plumule B. Radicle C. Cotyledon D. Hypocotyl Answer: B
In a germinating seed, what embryonic shoot tip gives rise to the future stem and leaves? A. Radicle B. Plumule (epicotyl) C. Coleoptile D. Micropyle Answer: B
What is the nutritive tissue of the developing embryo in angiosperm seeds called? A. Perisperm B. Endosperm (typically 3n, rich in starch, proteins, or lipids) C. Nucellus D. Hypocotyl Answer: B

What is recombinant DNA?

    Answer: Recombinant DNA is DNA formed by joining genetic material from different sources.

 What is tissue culture?

    Answer: Tissue culture is the growth of cells, tissues or organs on a sterile nutrient medium under controlled
    conditions.
content.long_questions:
Outline the main steps of recombinant DNA technology.

    Answer: A desired gene and a suitable vector are isolated. Restriction enzymes cut the DNA and vector at compatible
    sites. DNA ligase joins the gene to the vector, forming recombinant DNA. The recombinant vector is introduced into a
    host cell, selected and multiplied. The inserted gene may then be expressed and the product harvested. Controls and
    safety assessment are essential.

mcqs.content: What is totipotency in plant biology, established by Gottlieb Haberlandt (1902)? A. Cell death B. The inherent capacity of a single living plant cell to regenerate into a whole, complete fertile plant organism C. Ability to form spores D. Resistance to disease Answer: B

In plant tissue culture, what is the sterile piece of plant tissue excised for culture initiation called? A. Callus B. Explant (e.g., shoot tip, leaf disc, nodal segment) C. Inoculum D. Seedling Answer: B
In tissue culture, what is the unorganized, proliferating, undifferentiated mass of actively dividing parenchymatous cells called? A. Explant B. Callus C. Embryoid D. Protoplast Answer: B

What two classes of plant growth regulators (hormones) are adjusted in culture media to induce organogenesis (roots and shoots)? A. ABA and ethylene B. Auxin (induces roots at high auxin:cytokinin ratio) and Cytokinin (induces shoots at high cytokinin:auxin ratio) C. Gibberellin only D. Vitamins Answer: B

Which nutrient culture medium developed in 1962 is the most widely utilized formulation in plant tissue culture globally? A. White's medium B. MS medium (Murashige and Skoog medium) C. B5 medium D. Knop's solution Answer: B

What technique removes plant cell walls using cellulase and pectinase enzymes to enable somatic hybridization? A. Micropropagation B. Protoplast isolation and fusion C. Anther culture D. Meristem culture Answer: B

Why is apical meristem culture widely used in agriculture and horticulture? A. To produce polyploids B. To produce 100% virus-free pathogen-tested planting stocks (meristem tips lack vascular virus movement) C. To induce mutations D. To produce seedless fruits Answer: B

What is recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology (genetic engineering)? A. Selective breeding B. The joining together of DNA molecules from two different species to produce novel genetic combinations inserted into a host organism C. Natural hybridization D. Clonal propagation Answer: B

Which specialized enzymes act as 'molecular scissors' by cleaving DNA at specific symmetrical palindromic recognition sequences? A. DNA ligases B. Restriction endonucleases (e.g., EcoRI, HindIII, BamHI) C. DNA polymerases D. Helicases Answer: B

What enzyme acts as 'molecular glue' to covalently join complementary DNA fragments by synthesizing phosphodiester bonds? A. Restriction enzyme B. DNA Ligase C. RNA polymerase D. Reverse transcriptase Answer: B

What is the naturally occurring soil bacterium famous as 'Nature's Genetic Engineer' for transferring its Ti-plasmid into plant genomes? A. Escherichia coli B. Agrobacterium tumefaciens (causing crown gall disease) C. Bacillus thuringiensis D. Rhizobium leguminosarum Answer: B

What insecticidal crystal protein gene derived from soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis is engineered into Bt Cotton and Bt Brinjal? A. Cry gene (coding for Cry delta-endotoxin protein lethal to insect larvae) B. Nif gene C. Lac gene D. Bar gene Answer: A

What pest-resistant transgenic vegetable was successfully developed and commercially released in Bangladesh in 2013? A. Bt Tomato B. Bt Brinjal (eggplant resistant to fruit and shoot borer Leucinodes orbonalis) C. Golden Rice D. Bt Potato Answer: B

What biofortified transgenic crop was engineered with daffodil and Erwinia genes to produce beta-carotene (provitamin A) in rice endosperm? A. Bt Cotton B. Golden Rice C. Flavr Savr Tomato D. Roundup Ready Soy Answer: B

What molecular technique invented by Kary Mullis (1983) amplifies a specific segment of DNA into billions of copies in vitro in hours? A. Gel electrophoresis B. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) C. Northern blotting D. DNA sequencing Answer: B

Why is Taq DNA polymerase extracted from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus used in PCR? A. It is cheap B. It is thermostable and withstands repeated denaturation cycles at 95 °C without deactivation C. It has proofreading only D. It works at 0 °C Answer: B

What technique separates DNA fragments based on molecular size and charge across an agarose matrix in an electric field? A. Centrifugation B. Agarose Gel Electrophoresis (negatively charged DNA migrates toward positive anode) C. Chromatography D. PCR Answer: B

What fluorescent dye intercalates between DNA base pairs and fluoresces bright orange under ultraviolet (UV) illumination? A. Crystal violet B. Ethidium bromide (EtBr) C. Safranin D. Methylene blue Answer: B
In genetic engineering, what is the vehicle used to carry foreign DNA into a host cell (e.g. Plasmids, bacteriophages, cosmids) called? A. Antigen B. Cloning Vector C. Exon D. Operon Answer: B

content.short_questions:
What is bilateral symmetry?

    Answer: Bilateral symmetry means the body can be divided into two similar halves by only one longitudinal plane.

 What is a notochord?

    Answer: A notochord is a flexible supporting rod present at least during some stage of development in chordates.

Explain the importance of animal classification and name major bases used in it.

    Answer: Classification provides an organised system for identifying, naming and comparing animals. It helps

    notochord.

mcqs.content: What are animals possessing two embryonic germ layers (ectoderm and endoderm, e.g. Cnidaria) termed? A. Triploblastic B. Diploblastic C. Acoelomate D. Pseudocoelomate Answer: B

Animals possessing all three embryonic germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm) are termed: A. Diploblastic B. Triploblastic (from Platyhelminthes to Chordata) C. Monoblastic D. Radial Answer: B

What is a true coelom (eucoelom) in animal anatomy? A. Any body space B. A body cavity completely lined by mesodermal epithelium (peritoneum) located between body wall and gut C. Gut cavity D. Blastocoel Answer: B
Which invertebrate phylum is characterized by an acoelomate body plan (mesoderm forms solid parenchyma, no body cavity)? A. Nematoda B. Platyhelminthes (flatworms) C. Annelida D. Mollusca Answer: B

Which animal phylum possesses a false body cavity (pseudocoelom) derived from blastocoel and not lined by mesodermal peritoneum? A. Annelida B. Nematoda (roundworms, e.g. Ascaris lumbricoides) C. Arthropoda D. Platyhelminthes Answer: B

Which type of body symmetry divides an animal into identical halves along multiple radial planes passing through central axis (e.g. Hydra, jellyfish)? A. Bilateral symmetry B. Radial symmetry C. Asymmetry D. Biradial only Answer: B
Which phylum exhibits bilateral symmetry in larvae but secondary pentaradial symmetry in adults? A. Arthropoda B. Echinodermata (e.g. Starfish, sea urchin) C. Mollusca D. Cnidaria Answer: B

In animal taxonomy, what are the four diagnostic hallmark characteristics of the Phylum Chordata present at some life stage? A. Heart, lungs, legs, eyes B. Notochord, Dorsal hollow tubular nerve cord, Pharyngeal gill slits, and Post-anal tail C. Exoskeleton, antennae, open circulation D. Coelom, shell, mantle Answer: B
Which invertebrate phylum contains collar cells (choanocytes) and an internal water canal system with ostia and osculum? A. Cnidaria B. Porifera (sponges) C. Platyhelminthes D. Ctenophora Answer: B

Which phylum possesses specialized stinging cells (cnidocytes / nematocysts) and exists in polyp and medusa body forms? A. Porifera B. Cnidaria (e.g. Hydra, Obelia, Aurelia) C. Mollusca D. Echinodermata Answer: B

What is the largest phylum in the animal kingdom, characterized by chitinous exoskeleton and jointed appendages? A. Mollusca B. Arthropoda (constituting over 80% of all described animal species) C. Chordata D. Nematoda Answer: B
Which organ is the raspy, chitinous tongue-like feeding structure unique to the Phylum Mollusca (e.g. Snails, squid)? A. Radula B. Mantle C. Nephridium D. Ctenidium Answer: A

What unique organ system in Phylum Echinodermata functions in locomotion, food gathering, and gas exchange? A. Blood vascular system B. Water Vascular System (Ambulacral system with tube feet and madreporite) C. Tracheal system D. Nephridial system Answer: B

Which subphylum of Chordata retains a persistent notochord extending from head to tail throughout life (e.g. Branchiostoma / Amphioxus)? A. Urochordata B. Cephalochordata C. Vertebrata D. Hemichordata Answer: B

Birds (Class Aves) and Mammals (Class Mammalia) are warm-blooded vertebrates, scientifically termed: A. Poikilothermic B. Homeothermic (endothermic, maintaining constant internal body temperature) C. Ectothermic D. Heterothermic Answer: B

What are cnidocytes?

    Answer: Cnidocytes are specialised stinging cells of cnidarians that contain organelles called nematocysts.

 How does a grasshopper breathe?

    Answer: A grasshopper breathes through a tracheal system: air enters through spiracles and travels through tracheae
    and finer tracheoles.
content.long_questions:
Compare the respiratory systems of Hydra, grasshopper and rohu fish.

    Answer: Hydra has no specialised respiratory organ; gases diffuse directly across its body surface. Grasshopper uses
    a tracheal system in which air enters through spiracles and reaches tissues through tracheae and tracheoles. Rohu
    fish uses gills; water passes over gill surfaces where oxygen diffuses into blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out.

mcqs.content: Hydra is a freshwater carnivorous diploblastic cnidarian possessing which two body wall layers separated by mesoglea? A. Ectoderm and mesoderm B. Epidermis (outer) and Gastrodermis (inner), separated by non-cellular gelatinous Mesoglea C. Cuticle and hypodermis D. Cortex and medulla Answer: B
How many hollow tentacles surround the hypostome and mouth of Hydra viridissima? A. 2 to 4 B. 6 to 10 tentacles C. 20 to 30 D. 100 Answer: B

What is the most common and dangerous penetrating type of nematocyst in Hydra that injects poisonous hypnotoxin into prey? A. Volvent (desmoneme) B. Penetrant (stenotele, pear-shaped with three barbs and coiled thread) C. Glutinant (streptoline) D. Stereoline Answer: B

What type of locomotion in Hydra resembles looping or somersaulting over a substrate? A. Gliding and swimming B. Looping (measuring caterpillar movement) and Somersaulting C. Flying D. Jet propulsion Answer: B

What is the primary mode of asexual reproduction in Hydra when food and environmental conditions are plentiful? A. Fission B. Budding (formation of a lateral bud that develops tentacles, mouth, and detaches) C. Regeneration only D. Spore formation Answer: B
Who first discovered the remarkable regenerative capacity of Hydra in 1740? A. Robert Hooke B. Abraham Trembley (Trembley's polyp regeneration experiments) C. Leeuwenhoek D. Linnaeus Answer: B

What green unicellular zoochlorellae alga lives symbiotically inside the gastrodermal nutritive-muscular cells of green Hydra viridis? A. Chlamydomonas B. Chlorella vulgaris (Zoochlorella) C. Spirogyra D. Volvox Answer: B

The grasshopper (Poekilocerus pictus) belongs to which insect order characterized by straight, leathery forewings (tegmina) and jumping hind legs? A. Diptera B. Orthoptera C. Coleoptera D. Lepidoptera Answer: B
What type of compound eyes do grasshoppers possess composed of hundreds of individual hexagonal visual units called? A. Ocelli B. Ommatidia (singular: Ommatidium) C. Retinulae D. Rhabdomes Answer: B

What type of mouthparts does a grasshopper have adapted for feeding on leaves and vegetation? A. Siphoning type B. Biting and chewing (mandibulate) type C. Piercing and sucking D. Sponging type Answer: B

What is the main respiratory organ system of grasshoppers and insects consisting of spiracles and branching air tubes? A. Lungs B. Tracheal system (direct oxygen delivery without blood pigment) C. Book lungs D. Gills Answer: B
How many pairs of external respiratory spiracles (stigmata) are present on the body of a grasshopper? A. 5 pairs B. 10 pairs (2 pairs on thorax, 8 pairs on abdomen) C. 12 pairs D. 8 pairs Answer: B

What are the primary excretory organs of grasshoppers and insects located at the junction of midgut and hindgut? A. Nephridia B. Malpighian tubules (excreting uric acid, making them uricotelic) C. Green glands D. Flame cells Answer: B

What is the scientific name of the major freshwater carp fish Ruhu (Rohu)? A. Catla catla B. Labeo rohita (Hamilton, 1822) C. Cirrhinus mrigala D. Tenualosa ilisha Answer: B

What type of scales covers the body of a Ruhu fish (Labeo rohita)? A. Placoid scales B. Cycloid scales (thin, flexible, overlapping with concentric growth rings/annuli) C. Ctenoid scales D. Ganoid scales Answer: B

How many chambers are present in the venous, single-circulation heart of a bony fish like Ruhu? A. 3 chambers B. 2 chambers (1 atrium + 1 ventricle, plus sinus venosus and bulbus arteriosus) C. 4 chambers D. 1 chamber Answer: B

chapters.title: Human Physiology: Digestion and Absorption

content.overview:
Digestion breaks large food molecules into smaller absorbable units. The alimentary canal and accessory glands
 coordinate mechanical and chemical digestion, while the small intestine is the main site of nutrient absorption.
key_terms: Mechanical digestion increases food surface area; enzymes catalyse chemical digestion.
Salivary amylase begins starch digestion in the mouth.
The stomach secretes acid and enzymes; pepsin begins protein digestion.
Bile emulsifies fats but contains no digestive enzyme.
study_notes: Mechanical digestion increases food surface area; enzymes catalyse chemical digestion.
Salivary amylase begins starch digestion in the mouth.
The stomach secretes acid and enzymes; pepsin begins protein digestion.
Bile emulsifies fats but contains no digestive enzyme.
Villi and microvilli increase the absorptive surface of the small intestine.
content.short_questions:
What is peristalsis?

    Answer: Peristalsis is the coordinated wave-like contraction of smooth muscles that moves food along the alimentary
    canal.

 What is the function of bile?

    Answer: Bile emulsifies large fat globules into smaller droplets and helps provide an alkaline environment for intestinal
    digestion.
content.long_questions:
Describe digestion and absorption in the small intestine.

    Answer: The duodenum receives bile and pancreatic juice. Bile emulsifies fats; pancreatic enzymes digest
    carbohydrates, proteins and lipids. Intestinal enzymes complete digestion. Villi and microvilli provide a large surface
    area. Monosaccharides and amino acids enter blood capillaries, while most absorbed lipid products enter intestinal
    lacteals as part of chylomicrons.

mcqs.content: What digestive enzyme present in human saliva hydrolyzes cooked dietary starch into maltose? A. Pepsin B. Salivary amylase (Ptyalin) C. Trypsin D. Lipase Answer: B

Which specialized gastric gland cells in the stomach secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl) and intrinsic factor of Castle? A. Chief (peptic) cells B. Oxyntic (parietal) cells C. Mucous neck cells D. G cells Answer: B

What is the inactive zymogen precursor of the primary protein-digesting enzyme in gastric juice? A. Trypsinogen B. Pepsinogen (activated to active pepsin by HCl at optimal pH 1.5 - 2.0) C. Procarboxypeptidase D. Chymotrypsinogen Answer: B
What is intrinsic factor secreted by parietal cells essential for absorbing in the ileum? A. Iron B. Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) C. Calcium D. Vitamin C Answer: B
What is the largest internal gland and metabolic chemical factory of the human body? A. Pancreas B. Liver (~1.5 kg) C. Spleen D. Thyroid Answer: B

Where is bile continuously synthesized by hepatocytes and where is it stored and concentrated? A. Pancreas and duodenum B. Synthesized by liver hepatocytes, stored and concentrated in the Gallbladder C. Stomach and gallbladder D. Duodenum only Answer: B

Does bile contain any digestive enzymes? A. Yes, proteases B. No digestive enzymes (contains bile salts: sodium glycocholate and sodium taurocholate for emulsification of fats) C. Yes, lipases D. Yes, amylases Answer: B

What digestive juice secreted into the duodenum is called 'complete digestive juice' because it contains enzymes for all food groups? A. Gastric juice B. Pancreatic juice (contains trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, amylase, lipase, nucleases) C. Bile D. Saliva Answer: B
What brush-border duodenal enzyme converts inactive pancreatic trypsinogen into active trypsin? A. Pepsin B. Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) C. Secretin D. CCK Answer: B
Which pancreatic enzyme hydrolyzes dietary emulsified triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids? A. Pepsin B. Pancreatic lipase (Steapsin) C. Chymotrypsin D. Amylase Answer: B

What specialized anatomical microscopic finger-like projections in the small intestine enormously increase absorption surface area? A. Rugae B. Intestinal villi and microvilli (brush border) C. Cilia D. Flagella Answer: B
Inside each intestinal villus, what specialized central lymphatic capillary absorbs digested lipids and chylomicrons? A. Arteriole B. Lacteal (lymphatic vessel) C. Venule D. Nerve fiber Answer: B

Through which major blood vessel are water-soluble nutrients (glucose, amino acids) carried from the intestines directly to the liver? A. Hepatic artery B. Hepatic portal vein C. Inferior vena cava D. Renal vein Answer: B
The conversion of excess glucose into glycogen for storage in liver and muscle cells stimulated by insulin is called: A. Glycogenolysis B. Glycogenesis C. Gluconeogenesis D. Glycolysis Answer: B
The breakdown of stored liver glycogen into glucose stimulated by glucagon during fasting is called: A. Glycogenesis B. Glycogenolysis C. Gluconeogenesis D. Lipogenesis Answer: B
The synthesis of new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors (amino acids, glycerol, lactic acid) in the liver is called: A. Glycolysis B. Gluconeogenesis C. Glycogenesis D. Deamination Answer: B

What is the toxic metabolic byproduct of protein deamination converted to harmless urea in the liver's ornithine cycle? A. Uric acid B. Ammonia (NH3 converted to urea via Ornithine / Urea cycle) C. Creatinine D. Bilirubin Answer: B

What gastrointestinal hormone stimulated by acidic chyme in the duodenum triggers the pancreas to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid? A. Gastrin B. Secretin (the first hormone discovered by Bayliss and Starling, 1902) C. Cholecystokinin (CCK) D. GIP Answer: B

What gastrointestinal hormone triggers contraction of the gallbladder to eject bile and secretion of enzyme-rich pancreatic juice? A. Gastrin B. Cholecystokinin (CCK / pancreozymin) C. Secretin D. Motilin Answer: B

What is Body Mass Index (BMI) formula and what value range indicates a normal healthy adult weight? A. Weight / Height, 10-15 B. Weight (kg) / [Height (m)]^2; Normal range: 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m^2 C. Height / Weight, 25-30 D. Weight * Height, 50-60 Answer: B

 Chapter overview
 Digestion breaks large food molecules into smaller absorbable units. The alimentary canal and accessory glands

 Key terms

    Answer: Peristalsis is the coordinated wave-like contraction of smooth muscles that moves food along the alimentary
    canal.

    digestion.

content.short_questions:
What is haemoglobin?

    Answer: Haemoglobin is an iron-containing protein in red blood cells that binds and transports oxygen.

 What is double circulation?

    Answer: Double circulation means blood passes through the heart twice during one complete circuit: once through
    pulmonary circulation and once through systemic circulation.
content.long_questions:
Trace the pathway of blood through the human heart.

    Answer: Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium through the venae cavae, passes through the
    tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, and is pumped through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood
    returns through pulmonary veins to the left atrium, passes through the bicuspid/mitral valve to the left ventricle, and is
    pumped through the aorta to the body.

mcqs.content: What is the total volume and pH range of blood in a healthy adult human body? A. 3 liters, pH 6.0 B. 5 to 6 liters (~8% of body weight), slightly alkaline pH 7.35 to 7.45 C. 10 liters, pH 8.0 D. 4 liters, pH 5.5 Answer: B

What percentage of total blood volume is constituted by liquid blood plasma and formed cellular elements respectively? A. 80% and 20% B. 55% plasma and 45% formed elements (RBCs, WBCs, platelets) C. 50% and 50% D. 40% and 60% Answer: B

Which major plasma protein synthesized by the liver is primarily responsible for maintaining blood colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure? A. Fibrinogen B. Serum albumin C. Immunoglobulin G D. Prothrombin Answer: B
What is the average normal life span of human red blood cells (erythrocytes)? A. 10 days B. 120 days (~4 months, destroyed in spleen 'graveyard of RBCs') C. 30 days D. 1 year Answer: B
Where are all blood cells formed in adult humans through hematopoiesis? A. Liver only B. Red bone marrow (spongy bone) C. Spleen only D. Yellow bone marrow Answer: B

Which agranulocytic white blood cells are responsible for specific adaptive immunity by producing antibodies (plasma cells) and cell-mediated immunity? A. Neutrophils B. Lymphocytes (B cells and T cells) C. Monocytes D. Eosinophils Answer: B

Which white blood cells are the most abundant (60-70%) and act as the first line of phagocytic defense against bacterial infections? A. Basophils B. Neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leukocytes) C. Lymphocytes D. Eosinophils Answer: B
Which granulocytes release histamine (mediator of allergic and inflammatory reactions) and heparin (natural anticoagulant)? A. Neutrophils B. Basophils C. Eosinophils D. Monocytes Answer: B

What cell fragments derived from megakaryocytes are essential for primary hemostasis and blood clotting? A. Erythrocytes B. Platelets (Thrombocytes, normal count: 150,000 to 450,000 / mm3) C. Lymphocytes D. Reticulocytes Answer: B

In the blood clotting cascade, what active enzyme converts soluble plasma fibrinogen into an insoluble meshwork of fibrin fibers? A. Prothrombin B. Thrombin (with Ca2+ ions) C. Thromboplastin D. Heparin Answer: B

According to the ABO blood group system discovered by Karl Landsteiner (1900), a person with blood group AB has: A. Both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma B. Both A and B antigens on RBC surface, and NO antibodies in plasma (Universal recipient) C. Neither antigen D. Only anti-A antibody Answer: B
Which blood group is known as the 'Universal Donor' because its RBCs lack both A and B surface antigens? A. Group AB B. Group O (specifically O negative) C. Group A D. Group B Answer: B

What severe hemolytic disease of the newborn can occur in an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive second fetus? A. Hemophilia B. Erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of newborn prevented by Anti-D Rh immune globulin) C. Sickle cell anemia D. Thalassemia Answer: B

Which specialized neuromuscular tissue located in the right atrium acts as the natural 'Pacemaker of the Heart'? A. AV node B. Sinoatrial (SA) node (initiates rhythmic action potentials at 70-80 bpm) C. Bundle of His D. Purkinje fibers Answer: B

What is the complete electrical conduction pathway through the human heart? A. AV node -> SA node -> Purkinje fibers B. SA node -> AV node -> Bundle of His -> Left and Right Bundle Branches -> Purkinje fibers C. Purkinje fibers -> SA node D. Ventricle to atrium Answer: B

What does the P wave in a standard clinical Electrocardiogram (ECG) represent? A. Ventricular depolarization B. Atrial depolarization (atrial contraction / systole) C. Ventricular repolarization D. Atrial repolarization Answer: B
What does the QRS complex in an ECG trace represent? A. Atrial systole B. Ventricular depolarization (ventricular contraction / systole) C. Ventricular repolarization D. SA node firing Answer: B

What is the volume of blood pumped out by each ventricle per cardiac contraction (Stroke Volume, SV) in a resting adult? A. 20 mL B. 70 mL (~70 mL per beat, Cardiac Output = SV * HR ~ 5 L/min) C. 120 mL D. 500 mL Answer: B

What is considered normal healthy resting arterial blood pressure in a young adult human? A. 140/90 mmHg B. 120/80 mmHg (120 mmHg systolic / 80 mmHg diastolic) C. 100/60 mmHg D. 160/100 mmHg Answer: B

What surgical procedure bypasses blocked coronary arteries using a harvested vein (e.g. Saphenous vein) or artery to restore myocardial perfusion? A. Angioplasty B. Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG) C. Stenting alone D. Pacemaker implantation Answer: B

chapters.title: Human Physiology: Respiration and Breathing

content.overview:
Breathing moves air into and out of the lungs, while cellular respiration releases energy from nutrients. Gas exchange
 occurs across thin respiratory surfaces and is supported by ventilation and circulation.
key_terms: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens; thoracic volume increases.
Gas exchange in alveoli occurs by diffusion down partial-pressure gradients.
Oxygen is transported mainly bound to haemoglobin.
Carbon dioxide is transported mainly as bicarbonate ions in blood.
study_notes: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens; thoracic volume increases.
Gas exchange in alveoli occurs by diffusion down partial-pressure gradients.
Oxygen is transported mainly bound to haemoglobin.
Carbon dioxide is transported mainly as bicarbonate ions in blood.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide, water and ATP.
content.short_questions:
Distinguish breathing and cellular respiration.

    Answer: Breathing is the physical movement of air into and out of the lungs; cellular respiration is the series of
    chemical reactions that release energy from organic molecules in cells.

 Why are alveoli efficient for gas exchange?

    Answer: Alveoli provide a large surface area, thin moist walls, a rich capillary supply and ventilation that maintains
    diffusion gradients.
content.long_questions:
Explain the mechanism of inhalation and exhalation in humans.

    Answer: During quiet inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens and external intercostal muscles raise the ribs.
    Thoracic volume increases, intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure and air enters. During quiet
    exhalation, these muscles relax, thoracic volume decreases, pressure rises and air flows out. Forced breathing recruits
    additional muscles.

mcqs.content: What is the primary structural and functional microscopic unit of human lungs where alveolar gas exchange takes place? A. Bronchiole B. Alveolus (singular: Alveoli, ~300 million per lung providing 70-80 m2 surface area) C. Trachea D. Pleura Answer: B

What phospholipid-protein complex secreted by Type II alveolar pneumocytes lowers surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse during expiration? A. Mucus B. Pulmonary Surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) C. Hemoglobin D. Pleural fluid Answer: B

What double-layered serous membrane encloses and protects each lung, containing lubricating fluid between its visceral and parietal layers? A. Pericardium B. Pleura C. Peritoneum D. Meninges Answer: B

Inspiration (inhalation) during quiet resting breathing is an active muscular process primarily driven by contraction of: A. Abdominal muscles B. Diaphragm (flattens downward) and External Intercostal Muscles (elevate ribs) C. Internal intercostal muscles D. Pectoralis major Answer: B
What is the volume of air inspired or expired during normal quiet breathing (Tidal Volume, TV) in an adult human? A. 150 mL B. 500 mL (~0.5 liter) C. 1200 mL D. 3000 mL Answer: B

What is Vital Capacity (VC) of the human lungs defined as? A. Tidal volume only B. The maximum volume of air that can be expired following a maximal inspiration (VC = TV + IRV + ERV ~ 4.5 liters) C. Total lung capacity D. Residual volume Answer: B

What is Residual Volume (RV) of the lungs that remains inside alveoli even after forceful maximal expiration? A. Zero B. 1100 to 1200 mL (prevents lungs from ever collapsing completely) C. 500 mL D. 2500 mL Answer: B

How is the vast majority (approximately 97%) of oxygen transported in human arterial blood? A. Dissolved in plasma water B. Reversibly bound to hemoglobin inside red blood cells as Oxyhemoglobin (Hb4O8) C. As bicarbonate ions D. As carbamino compounds Answer: B
How many molecules of oxygen (O2) can one molecule of fully saturated hemoglobin bind to its four iron-containing heme groups? A. 1 B. 4 molecules of O2 (one per Fe2+ atom) C. 2 D. 8 Answer: B

What is the primary form (approximately 70%) in which carbon dioxide (CO2) is transported in human blood? A. Dissolved gas in plasma (7%) B. As Bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) dissolved in blood plasma C. Carbaminohemoglobin (23%) D. Carbonic acid Answer: B
What rapid zinc-containing metalloenzyme in red blood cells catalyzes the reversible hydration of CO2 into carbonic acid (H2CO3)? A. Pepsin B. Carbonic Anhydrase C. Catalase D. Amylase Answer: B

What is the Chloride Shift (Hamburger phenomenon) in erythrocytic CO2 transport? A. Chloride enters lungs B. Diffusion of bicarbonate (HCO3-) out into plasma and inward exchange diffusion of chloride ions (Cl-) into RBCs to maintain electrical neutrality C. Loss of chloride in urine D. Active transport of sodium Answer: B

The Bohr Effect describes the decrease in hemoglobin's oxygen-binding affinity (shift of oxygen-dissociation curve to the right) caused by: A. Low temperature B. Increased CO2 partial pressure, decreased pH (acidity), and increased temperature in metabolically active tissues C. High oxygen concentration D. Decreased 2,3-BPG Answer: B

The Haldane Effect describes how deoxygenation of hemoglobin in tissues increases its capacity to: A. Release O2 B. Bind and carry carbon dioxide (CO2) C. Bind carbon monoxide D. Dissolve in plasma Answer: B

Where is the primary involuntary respiratory rhythmicity center located in the human brain? A. Cerebellum B. Medulla Oblongata (and Pons varolii: pneumotaxic center) C. Hypothalamus D. Cerebral cortex Answer: B

What is the primary chemical stimulus driving respiratory rate and ventilation under normal resting physiological conditions? A. Arterial oxygen depletion B. Arterial CO2 partial pressure (PCO2) and hydrogen ion concentration [H+] in CSF detected by central chemoreceptors C. Nitrogen level D. Blood pressure Answer: B

Which respiratory condition is characterized by chronic inflammation, smooth muscle bronchospasm, and wheezing in response to allergens? A. Tuberculosis B. Bronchial Asthma C. Pneumonia D. Emphysema Answer: B

Which chronic progressive lung disease caused by cigarette smoking is characterized by permanent destruction of alveolar walls and loss of elastic recoil? A. Asthma B. Pulmonary Emphysema (COPD) C. Pneumonia D. Pleurisy Answer: B

Why is carbon monoxide (CO) gas extremely lethal even in minute concentrations in inhaled air? A. It destroys alveoli B. Its affinity for hemoglobin is over 200 to 250 times higher than that of oxygen, forming stable carboxyhemoglobin and causing tissue hypoxia C. It irritates the trachea D. It causes coughing Answer: B

What is the anatomical structure preventing food and liquid from accidentally entering the larynx and trachea during swallowing? A. Uvula B. Epiglottis (elastic cartilaginous flap) C. Vocal cord D. Thyroid cartilage Answer: B

chapters.title: Human Physiology: Waste and Excretion

content.overview:
Excretion removes metabolic wastes and helps regulate water, salts and pH. In humans, kidneys filter blood and form
 urine through filtration, reabsorption and secretion.
key_terms: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
Ultrafiltration occurs at the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule.
Selective reabsorption returns useful substances and much water to blood.
Tubular secretion transfers selected substances from blood into the nephron.
study_notes: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
Ultrafiltration occurs at the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule.
Selective reabsorption returns useful substances and much water to blood.
Tubular secretion transfers selected substances from blood into the nephron.
ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts and helps regulate urine concentration.
content.short_questions:
What is a nephron?

    Answer: A nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney, consisting of a renal corpuscle and renal tubule.

 What is ultrafiltration?

    Answer: Ultrafiltration is pressure-driven filtration of water and small solutes from glomerular blood into Bowman's
    capsule.
content.long_questions:
Describe the main steps of urine formation.

    Answer: Blood is filtered under pressure in the glomerulus, forming filtrate in Bowman's capsule. Along the renal
    tubule, useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, ions and much water are selectively reabsorbed. Additional
    ions and wastes may be secreted into the tubule. The collecting ducts adjust water reabsorption, and the final urine
    passes to the renal pelvis, ureter and bladder.

mcqs.content: What is the primary nitrogenous excretory waste product excreted in human urine synthesized in the liver from ammonia? A. Ammonia B. Urea (making humans ureotelic organisms) C. Uric acid D. Creatinine Answer: B
What is the functional, structural microscopic filtration unit of the human kidney (~1 to 1.2 million per kidney)? A. Neuron B. Nephron C. Renal lobule D. Glomerulus only Answer: B

What two structures compose the Renal (Malpighian) Corpuscle where ultrafiltration occurs? A. Proximal tubule and Loop of Henle B. Glomerulus (capillary tuft) and Bowman's capsule (double-walled cup) C. Collecting duct and distal tubule D. Cortex and medulla Answer: B

What specialized epithelial cells with interdigitating foot processes (pedicels) form the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule? A. Endothelial cells B. Podocytes (forming microscopic filtration slits) C. Mesangial cells D. Macula densa Answer: B
What is the normal Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) in a healthy adult human (~180 liters of filtrate per day)? A. 50 mL/min B. 120 to 125 mL/min C. 500 mL/min D. 10 mL/min Answer: B

What percentage of the 180 liters of glomerular filtrate formed daily is reabsorbed back into peritubular capillaries? A. 50% B. Over 99% (~99.2%, resulting in ~1.5 liters of excreted urine per day) C. 80% D. 10% Answer: B

Where does the obligatory reabsorption of 65-70% of water, all glucose, and all amino acids occur via active transport in the nephron? A. Distal Convoluted Tubule B. Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT, with extensive brush border microvilli) C. Loop of Henle D. Collecting duct Answer: B

The hairpin-shaped Loop of Henle, with descending limb permeable to water and ascending limb pumping NaCl, functions as a: A. Filtration sieve B. Countercurrent Multiplier system (generating high osmotic gradient in renal medullary interstitium) C. Secretory canal D. Storage reservoir Answer: B

What specialized hairpin-shaped vascular loops parallel to the Loop of Henle act as a countercurrent exchanger to preserve medullary hypertonicity? A. Glomerulus B. Vasa Recta (capillaries) C. Renal vein D. Arcuate artery Answer: B

Which peptide hormone secreted by the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) increases water permeability in collecting ducts to conserve water? A. Aldosterone B. Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH / Vasopressin) C. Renin D. ANP Answer: B

A deficiency in the secretion of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) leads to excessive urination (polyuria) without sugar, a condition known as: A. Diabetes mellitus B. Diabetes insipidus C. Addison disease D. Cushing syndrome Answer: B
Which mineralocorticoid hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex stimulates active reabsorption of Na+ and excretion of K+ in the DCT? A. Cortisol B. Aldosterone C. Epinephrine D. Thyroxine Answer: B

What enzyme is released by the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells of the kidney in response to reduced renal perfusion pressure or low blood Na+? A. Angiotensin II B. Renin (initiating the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System, RAAS) C. Erythropoietin D. ACE Answer: B
What hormone produced by the kidneys in response to renal hypoxia stimulates red blood cell production in bone marrow? A. Renin B. Erythropoietin (EPO) C. Thrombopoietin D. Calcitriol Answer: B
What is the characteristic amber yellow color of normal human urine due to? A. Bile salts B. Urochrome (urobilin, a metabolic breakdown product of hemoglobin) C. Urea D. Melanin Answer: B
What is the average daily volume and pH of normal human urine? A. 5 L, pH 8.0 B. 1.0 to 1.5 liters per day, slightly acidic (average pH ~6.0, range 4.5-8.0) C. 0.5 L, pH 3.0 D. 3 L, pH 7.4 Answer: B

What is hemodialysis used in renal failure (uremia)? A. Kidney transplantation B. An artificial extracorporeal procedure where blood is pumped through a dialyzer membrane to remove urea, creatinine, and toxins C. Ultrasound therapy D. Surgical removal of kidney Answer: B

What non-invasive clinical technique uses focused acoustic shock waves to pulverize renal calculi (kidney stones) into fine gravel? A. Hemodialysis B. Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL) C. Laparoscopy D. Catheterization Answer: B
What is the primary chemical constituent of the most common type (~80%) of kidney stones (renal calculi)? A. Uric acid B. Calcium oxalate (and calcium phosphate) C. Cystine D. Struvite Answer: B

What triangular smooth muscular area on the floor of the urinary bladder is bounded by the two ureteric orifices and internal urethral meatus? A. Fundus B. Trigone of the bladder C. Neck D. Apex Answer: B

chapters.title: Human Physiology: Locomotion and Movement

content.short_questions:
What is a tendon?

    Answer: A tendon is a tough connective tissue that attaches muscle to bone.

 What is an antagonistic muscle pair?

    Answer: It is a pair of muscles that produce opposite movements; when one contracts, the other generally relaxes.
content.long_questions:
Explain the sliding-filament mechanism of skeletal muscle contraction.

    Answer: A nerve impulse triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium binds to troponin, shifting
    tropomyosin and exposing binding sites on actin. Myosin heads bind to actin and perform power strokes using energy
    from ATP, pulling thin filaments inward. Repeated cross-bridge cycles shorten the sarcomere. Calcium reuptake allows
    relaxation.

mcqs.content: How many bones compose the complete adult human skeletal system? A. 206 bones (80 axial + 126 appendicular) B. 300 bones C. 150 bones D. 250 bones Answer: A
How many bones constitute the axial skeleton of adult humans (cranium, facial, vertebral column, ribs, sternum)? A. 126 B. 80 bones C. 60 D. 100 Answer: B

How many total vertebrae form the human adult vertebral column? A. 26 vertebrae (7 Cervical, 12 Thoracic, 5 Lumbar, 1 Sacrum fused, 1 Coccyx fused) B. 33 vertebrae C. 24 vertebrae D. 30 vertebrae Answer: A
What is the first cervical vertebra (C1) that articulates with the occipital condyles of the skull permitting nodding 'yes' called? A. Axis B. Atlas (C1) C. Prominens D. Sacrum Answer: B
What is the second cervical vertebra (C2) bearing the odontoid process (dens) enabling head rotation ('no') called? A. Atlas B. Axis (C2) C. Thoracic D. Coccyx Answer: B

How many pairs of ribs are present in the human thoracic cage, and how are they classified? A. 10 pairs B. 12 pairs (7 pairs True ribs, 3 pairs False ribs, 2 pairs Floating ribs) C. 14 pairs D. 12 pairs all true Answer: B

Which ribs are called 'floating ribs' because their anterior ends do not attach to the sternum or costal cartilage? A. 1st and 2nd B. 11th and 12th pairs of ribs C. 8th, 9th, 10th D. 7th pair Answer: B
What is the longest, heaviest, and strongest tubular bone in the entire human body? A. Humerus B. Femur (thigh bone) C. Tibia D. Fibula Answer: B
What is the patella commonly known as, and what type of bone is it? A. Shin bone B. Kneecap; a sesamoid bone developed inside the quadriceps femoris tendon C. Ankle bone D. Pelvic bone Answer: B
What tough, fibrous, non-elastic connective tissue bands connect skeletal muscles to bones? A. Ligaments B. Tendons C. Cartilage D. Aponeuroses Answer: B
What strong, elastic bands of dense connective tissue connect bone to bone at synovial joints to stabilize joints? A. Tendons B. Ligaments C. Fascia D. Synovial fluid Answer: B

What type of freely movable synovial joint allows rotational movement in all planes (e.g. Shoulder joint and hip joint)? A. Hinge joint B. Ball-and-socket joint (spheroidal joint) C. Pivot joint D. Saddle joint Answer: B

What type of synovial joint allows angular movement predominantly in one plane like a door hinge (e.g. Elbow, knee)? A. Ball-and-socket B. Hinge joint (ginglymus) C. Gliding joint D. Pivot joint Answer: B

What microscopic repeating structural and functional contractile unit of a skeletal muscle myofibril spans between two Z-lines? A. Sarcolemma B. Sarcomere C. Sarcoplasmic reticulum D. Myofilament Answer: B

According to the Sliding Filament Theory of muscle contraction (Huxley and Hanson, 1954): A. Thick and thin filaments contract and shorten B. Thin actin filaments slide inward past thick myosin filaments toward the M-line, shortening the sarcomere and H-zone C. Myosin filaments stretch D. Z-lines move apart Answer: B
What key ion released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to troponin C, unmasking the myosin-binding sites on actin? A. Na+ ion B. Calcium ion (Ca2+) C. K+ ion D. Mg2+ ion Answer: B

What direct chemical energy currency is required for both the detachment of myosin cross-bridges and pumping Ca2+ back into sarcoplasmic reticulum? A. Creatine B. Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) C. Glucose D. Lactic acid Answer: B

content.overview:
The nervous and endocrine systems coordinate body activities. The nervous system uses rapid electrical signals, while
 hormones carried in blood generally produce slower and longer-lasting effects.
key_terms: A neuron consists of a cell body, dendrites and an axon.
A reflex arc provides a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus.
The central nervous system includes the brain and spinal cord.
Endocrine glands release hormones into blood; target cells possess suitable receptors.
study_notes: A neuron consists of a cell body, dendrites and an axon.

content.short_questions:
What is a reflex action?

    Answer: A reflex action is a rapid, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus, commonly coordinated through a
    reflex arc.

 What is a hormone?

    Answer: A hormone is a chemical messenger released by an endocrine cell or gland that acts on target cells with
    appropriate receptors.
content.long_questions:
Describe the pathway of a simple reflex arc.

    Answer: A receptor detects a stimulus and generates an impulse. A sensory neuron carries it to the spinal cord, where
    it communicates through one or more synapses, often involving an interneuron. A motor neuron carries the signal to an
    effector such as a muscle or gland. The effector produces the response; the brain is informed and may modify later
    behaviour.

mcqs.content: What is the structural and functional cellular communicating unit of the nervous system? A. Nephron B. Neuron (consisting of cell body / cyton, dendrites, and axon) C. Glial cell D. Synapse Answer: B

What lipid-rich insulating sheath wrapping myelinated axons in the peripheral nervous system is produced by Schwann cells? A. Neurilemma B. Myelin sheath (with periodic gaps called Nodes of Ranvier) C. Axolemma D. Endoneurium Answer: B

In myelinated nerve fibers, the rapid, jumping propagation of nerve impulses from one Node of Ranvier to the next is termed: A. Continuous conduction B. Saltatory conduction (much faster and energy-efficient) C. Electrotonic conduction D. Synaptic delay Answer: B

What is the resting membrane potential (RMP) of an unstimulated mammalian neuron? A. +30 mV B. -70 mV (inside negative relative to outside, maintained by Na+/K+ ATPase pump) C. 0 mV D. -90 mV Answer: B

During the rising phase of an action potential (depolarization), what voltage-gated ion channels open rapidly? A. K+ channels B. Voltage-gated Sodium (Na+) channels (causing rapid influx of Na+ into axon) C. Cl- channels D. Ca2+ channels Answer: B

What is the specialized microscopic junction across which a nerve impulse is transmitted chemically from one neuron to the next? A. Node of Ranvier B. Synapse (synaptic cleft) C. Neuromuscular junction D. Gap junction Answer: B
What major neurotransmitter is released at cholinergic synapses, autonomic ganglia, and neuromuscular junctions? A. Dopamine B. Acetylcholine (ACh) C. Serotonin D. GABA Answer: B

What is the largest, most highly developed part of the human brain responsible for conscious thought, voluntary movement, and memory? A. Cerebellum B. Cerebrum (cerebral cortex with four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital) C. Medulla oblongata D. Thalamus Answer: B
Which brain region, commonly called the 'little brain', coordinates voluntary muscle contractions, posture, balance, and equilibrium? A. Cerebrum B. Cerebellum C. Pons D. Hypothalamus Answer: B
What master neuroendocrine center of the brain regulates body temperature, thirst, hunger, sleep, and controls the pituitary gland? A. Thalamus B. Hypothalamus C. Epithalamus D. Hippocampus Answer: B

Which endocrine gland located in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone is historically termed the 'Master Gland' of the endocrine system? A. Thyroid gland B. Pituitary gland (Hypophysis) C. Adrenal gland D. Pancreas Answer: B

Which endocrine gland situated in the anterior neck secretes thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) regulating basal metabolic rate (BMR)? A. Pituitary B. Thyroid gland (follicular cells) C. Parathyroid D. Adrenal Answer: B

Dietary deficiency of which essential micronutrient causes enlargement of the thyroid gland, clinically known as endemic simple goiter? A. Iron B. Iodine (necessary for T3/T4 synthesis) C. Calcium D. Zinc Answer: B

Which peptide hormone secreted by the beta cells of the Islets of Langerhans lowers blood glucose concentration? A. Glucagon B. Insulin (facilitates cellular glucose uptake and glycogenesis) C. Somatostatin D. Epinephrine Answer: B
Which hormone secreted by the alpha cells of the Islets of Langerhans elevates blood glucose via glycogenolysis in the liver? A. Insulin B. Glucagon C. Cortisol D. Thyroxine Answer: B
Which hormone secreted by the adrenal medulla is known as the 'Emergency / Fight-or-Flight Hormone'? A. Aldosterone B. Epinephrine (Adrenaline) and Norepinephrine C. Cortisol D. Melatonin Answer: B

What photoreceptor cells in the human retina are responsible for daylight high-acuity color vision? A. Rod cells B. Cone cells (containing photopsin pigments for red, green, and blue light) C. Bipolar cells D. Ganglion cells Answer: B

What photoreceptor cells in the human retina containing the photopigment rhodopsin are responsible for vision in dim twilight (scotopic vision)? A. Cone cells B. Rod cells C. Amacrine cells D. Pigment cells Answer: B

What is the small coiled, fluid-filled snail-like organ of the inner ear containing the Organ of Corti responsible for hearing? A. Semicircular canals B. Cochlea C. Vestibule D. Tympanic membrane Answer: B

What structures in the inner ear containing endolymph and hair cell ampullae are responsible for detecting dynamic rotational balance? A. Cochlea B. Semicircular canals (three mutually perpendicular canals) C. Utricle and Saccule D. Eustachian tube Answer: B
