chapters.title: Continuity of Human Life (Reproduction)

content.overview:
Human reproduction involves the formation of gametes, fertilisation, implantation, embryonic development, birth and
 parental care. The reproductive systems are regulated by hormones.
key_terms: Spermatogenesis occurs in seminiferous tubules; oogenesis occurs in ovarian follicles.
The menstrual cycle involves coordinated changes in the ovaries and uterine lining.
Fertilisation normally occurs in the oviduct and forms a diploid zygote.
The embryo implants in the uterine endometrium.
study_notes: Spermatogenesis occurs in seminiferous tubules; oogenesis occurs in ovarian follicles.
The menstrual cycle involves coordinated changes in the ovaries and uterine lining.
Fertilisation normally occurs in the oviduct and forms a diploid zygote.
The embryo implants in the uterine endometrium.
The placenta enables exchange between maternal and fetal circulations without normally mixing their blood directly.
content.short_questions:
What is fertilisation?

    Answer: Fertilisation is the fusion of a haploid male gamete and a haploid female gamete to form a diploid zygote.

 What is the placenta?

    Answer: The placenta is a temporary organ that supports exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes between maternal
    and fetal blood and also produces hormones.
content.long_questions:
Outline the major events from fertilisation to implantation.

    Answer: A sperm penetrates the secondary oocyte and the nuclei ultimately unite to form a diploid zygote. The zygote
    undergoes cleavage divisions as it moves through the oviduct, forming a morula and then a blastocyst. The blastocyst
    reaches the uterus and attaches to, then embeds in, the endometrium during implantation.

mcqs.content: Where does spermatogenesis (sperm production) take place within the male testes? A. Epididymis B. Seminiferous tubules (germinal epithelium) C. Vas deferens D. Prostate gland Answer: B

Which interstitial cells located between the seminiferous tubules secrete the primary male androgen testosterone? A. Sertoli cells B. Leydig cells (Interstitial cells of Leydig) C. Spermatogonia D. Spermatids Answer: B

Which specialized somatic cells inside seminiferous tubules provide physical support, protection, and nourishment to developing spermatids? A. Leydig cells B. Sertoli cells (nurse cells forming blood-testis barrier) C. Macrophage D. Fibroblast Answer: B

What cap-like organelle covering the anterior half of the sperm head contains hydrolytic enzymes (hyaluronidase, acrosin) to penetrate ovum? A. Centriole B. Acrosome (derived from Golgi apparatus) C. Middle piece D. Flagellum Answer: B

Where are mature spermatozoa stored and undergo functional maturation and acquisition of forward motility? A. Rete testis B. Epididymis (~6 meters long coiled duct) C. Vas deferens D. Seminal vesicle Answer: B
Where does human fertilization (fusion of sperm and ovum to form zygote) normally take place? A. Uterine cavity B. Ampulla of the Fallopian tube (Oviduct) C. Ovary surface D. Cervix Answer: B

What is the average duration of a normal human menstrual cycle, and on which day does ovulation typically occur in a 28-day cycle? A. 20 days, day 5 B. 28 days, day 14 (triggered by LH surge) C. 35 days, day 21 D. 28 days, day 1 Answer: B

What temporary endocrine structure develops from the ruptured Graafian follicle after ovulation and secretes large amounts of progesterone? A. Corpus albicans B. Corpus luteum C. Corpus callosum D. Antrum Answer: B

What is the thick, highly vascularized mucosal inner lining of the uterus that is cyclically shed during menstruation? A. Perimetrium B. Endometrium (functional layer) C. Myometrium D. Cervix Answer: B

What hormone secreted by the trophoblast of the implanted blastocyst maintains the corpus luteum and is detected in home pregnancy urine tests? A. Estrogen B. Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) C. Progesterone D. Oxytocin Answer: B

At what developmental stage (~6 to 7 days post-fertilization) does the human embryo embed and implant into the uterine endometrium? A. Morula (solid ball) B. Blastocyst (hollow sphere with inner cell mass and trophoblast) C. Gastrula D. Neurula Answer: B

What temporary discoid fetomaternal organ facilitates nutrient uptake, gas exchange, and waste elimination between mother and fetus? A. Amnion B. Placenta (and umbilical cord) C. Yolk sac D. Allantois Answer: B

Which extraembryonic fluid-filled membrane cushions and protects the developing human fetus from mechanical shocks and desiccation? A. Chorion B. Amnion (containing amniotic fluid) C. Allantois D. Yolk sac Answer: B

What is the normal human gestation period (duration of pregnancy) from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP)? A. 200 days B. 280 days (~40 weeks / 9 calendar months) C. 365 days D. 150 days Answer: B

Which posterior pituitary hormone stimulates powerful rhythmic contractions of uterine myometrium during labor and milk ejection? A. Prolactin B. Oxytocin ('love hormone' / 'labor hormone') C. Progesterone D. Estrogen Answer: B
Which anterior pituitary hormone stimulates the synthesis and production of milk in mammary glands? A. Oxytocin B. Prolactin (PRL) C. hCG D. LH Answer: B

What is the initial thin, yellowish antibody-rich milk produced by the mother during the first few days post-partum called? A. Mature milk B. Colostrum (rich in maternal secretory IgA antibodies providing passive immunity) C. Casein D. Whey Answer: B
What is the permanent surgical contraception method in human males involving bilateral ligation and division of the vas deferens? A. Tubectomy B. Vasectomy C. Laparoscopy D. Castration Answer: B

What is the permanent surgical contraception method in human females involving bilateral cutting and ligating of the Fallopian tubes? A. Vasectomy B. Tubectomy (Tubal ligation) C. Hysterectomy D. Oophorectomy Answer: B

What assistive reproductive technology (ART) procedure fertilizes eggs with sperm outside the human body in a laboratory culture dish? A. IUI B. In Vitro Fertilization (IVF, 'test tube baby' pioneered by Edwards and Steptoe, 1978) C. ZIFT only D. Surrogacy Answer: B

chapters.title: Defence of the Human Body (Immunity)

content.overview:
The immune system protects the body against pathogens and abnormal cells. Innate immunity provides rapid general
 defence, while adaptive immunity develops specific responses and immunological memory.
key_terms: Physical barriers include skin and mucous membranes.
Phagocytes engulf pathogens; inflammation helps recruit immune cells.
B lymphocytes can differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory cells.
T lymphocytes coordinate immune responses or destroy infected cells.
study_notes: Physical barriers include skin and mucous membranes.
Phagocytes engulf pathogens; inflammation helps recruit immune cells.
B lymphocytes can differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory cells.
T lymphocytes coordinate immune responses or destroy infected cells.
Vaccination exposes the immune system to an antigen safely enough to promote immune memory.
content.short_questions:
What is an antigen?

    Answer: An antigen is a substance recognised by the immune system that can trigger a specific immune response.

 What is immunological memory?

    Answer: Immunological memory is the ability of the adaptive immune system to respond more rapidly and strongly
    after a previous exposure to an antigen.
content.long_questions:
Compare innate and adaptive immunity.

    Answer: Innate immunity is present from birth, responds rapidly and recognises broad classes of threats. It includes
    barriers, phagocytes, inflammation and complement. Adaptive immunity is antigen-specific, involves B and T
    lymphocytes, develops after exposure and forms memory cells. This memory allows a faster, stronger response on
    subsequent exposure.

mcqs.content: What is the body's first line of innate immune defense against pathogen invasion? A. Antibodies B. Physical and chemical barriers (intact skin, mucous membranes, stomach HCl, lysozyme in tears) C. T-killer cells D. Memory cells Answer: B
What antibacterial enzyme found in human tears, saliva, and sweat hydrolyzes bacterial peptidoglycan cell walls? A. Pepsin B. Lysozyme C. Amylase D. Lipase Answer: B

What are the key cellular components of the body's second line of non-specific innate defense? A. B cells B. Phagocytic white blood cells (Neutrophils and Macrophages), Natural Killer (NK) cells, and inflammatory response C. Erythrocytes D. Plasma cells Answer: B

What family of antiviral signaling glycoproteins is secreted by virus-infected host cells to protect neighboring uninfected cells? A. Histamines B. Interferons (IFN-alpha, IFN-beta, IFN-gamma) C. Antibodies D. Perforins Answer: B

What is an antigen (immunogen) in immunology? A. An antibiotic B. Any foreign substance (protein or polysaccharide) capable of stimulating a specific immune response and binding to antibodies C. A white blood cell D. A vaccine adjuvant Answer: B

What are the specialized Y-shaped protective glycoprotein molecules synthesized by activated B-cell plasma cells called? A. Antigens B. Antibodies (Immunoglobulins, Ig) C. Interferons D. Complements Answer: B

How many polypeptide chains constitute a monomeric antibody molecule (e.g. IgG)? A. 2 chains B. 4 polypeptide chains (2 identical Heavy chains + 2 identical Light chains connected by disulfide bonds: H2L2) C. 6 chains D. 1 chain Answer: B

What is the antigen-binding variable fragment of an antibody molecule designated as? A. Fc region B. Fab region (Fragment antigen-binding, containing the variable paratope) C. Hinge region D. Constant domain Answer: B
Which immunoglobulin class is the most abundant in human serum (~80%) and the only antibody that crosses the placenta to protect the fetus? A. IgM B. IgG (Immunoglobulin G) C. IgA D. IgE Answer: B
Which immunoglobulin class is secreted as a dimer into body secretions (colostrum, breast milk, saliva, tears, intestinal mucus)? A. IgG B. IgA (Secretory IgA) C. IgE D. IgD Answer: B
Which immunoglobulin class is the largest (pentamer with J-chain) and is the first antibody synthesized in primary immune response? A. IgG B. IgM (Macroglobulin) C. IgA D. IgE Answer: B
Which immunoglobulin class mediates immediate Type I hypersensitivity (allergic reactions) by binding to Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils? A. IgA B. IgE C. IgG D. IgM Answer: B

What are the two major functional subtypes of T lymphocytes in cell-mediated adaptive immunity? A. Neutrophils and basophils B. Helper T cells (CD4+ T cells, orchestrate immune response) and Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+ CTLs, destroy infected cells) C. B cells and plasma cells D. NK cells and monocytes Answer: B

What cell surface protein molecule on Helper T cells is the primary receptor targeted by HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus)? A. CD8 B. CD4 receptor (leading to progressive depletion of CD4+ T cells and AIDS) C. CD3 D. MHC Class I Answer: B

What type of immunity is acquired by an infant through receiving maternal antibodies via the placenta and breast milk (colostrum)? A. Active artificial B. Natural Passive Immunity (provides immediate temporary protection) C. Natural active D. Artificial active Answer: B

What type of immunity is induced by administering an approved vaccine (e.g. Polio, Measles, Hepatitis B)? A. Passive natural B. Artificial Active Immunity (stimulates host immune system to produce long-lasting memory B and T cells) C. Artificial passive D. Innate Answer: B

What was the first successful vaccine in human medical history, developed by Edward Jenner in 1796 against smallpox? A. Rabies vaccine B. Smallpox vaccine (using cowpox virus) C. Polio vaccine D. BCG vaccine Answer: B

What type of vaccine is the BCG vaccine used to protect against tuberculosis? A. Inactivated toxin B. Live attenuated bacterial vaccine (Bacillus Calmette-Guerin derived from attenuated Mycobacterium bovis) C. mRNA vaccine D. Recombinant subunit Answer: B

What are monoclonal antibodies produced by hybridoma technology (Kohler and Milstein, 1975)? A. Polyclonal antibodies B. Identical antibodies originating from a single B-cell clone fused with myeloma tumor cell, targeting one specific epitope C. Antibiotics D. Synthetic enzymes Answer: B

What condition occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the body's own healthy tissues (loss of self-tolerance)? A. Immunodeficiency B. Autoimmune disease (e.g. Systemic lupus erythematosus, Type 1 diabetes, Rheumatoid arthritis) C. Allergy D. Graft rejection Answer: B

 • B lymphocytes can differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory cells.

 • T lymphocytes coordinate immune responses or destroy infected cells.

 • Vaccination exposes the immune system to an antigen safely enough to promote immune memory.

    after a previous exposure to an antigen.

    Answer: Innate immunity is present from birth, responds rapidly and recognises broad classes of threats. It includes

    subsequent exposure.

mcqs.content: Who is universally recognized as the 'Father of Modern Genetics' for his pioneering pea plant hybridization experiments (1865)? A. Charles Darwin B. Gregor Johann Mendel C. Thomas Hunt Morgan D. James Watson Answer: B

What is Mendel's First Law of Inheritance (Law of Segregation)? A. Alleles blend together B. The two alleles for a heritable trait segregate during gamete formation so that each gamete carries only one allele C. Genes assort independently D. Dominance is absolute Answer: B

What is the expected phenotypic monohybrid ratio in the F2 generation of a complete dominance cross (e.g. Tall x Dwarf)? A. 1 : 2 : 1 B. 3 : 1 (3 dominant : 1 recessive) C. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 D. 1 : 1 Answer: B
What is the genotypic ratio in the F2 generation of Mendel's monohybrid cross? A. 3 : 1 B. 1 : 2 : 1 (1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt) C. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 D. 2 : 1 Answer: B

In incomplete dominance (e.g. Four o'clock plant Mirabilis jalapa, Red x White -> Pink), what is the F2 phenotypic ratio? A. 3 : 1 B. 1 : 2 : 1 (1 Red : 2 Pink : 1 White) C. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 D. 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 Answer: B

In codominance (e.g. AB blood group, roan cattle coat), both alleles are simultaneously and fully expressed in the heterozygote; what is the F2 ratio? A. 3 : 1 B. 1 : 2 : 1 C. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 D. 1 : 1 Answer: B
What is a lethal gene (e.g. Yellow fur in mice discovered by Lucien Cuenot) that causes homozygous embryo death, modifying the monohybrid ratio to: A. 3 : 1 B. 2 : 1 C. 1 : 2 : 1 D. 1 : 1 Answer: B

What is Mendel's Second Law of Inheritance (Law of Independent Assortment)? A. Alleles segregate into gametes B. Alleles of two or more different genes assort independently of one another into gametes during meiosis C. Genes on same chromosome stay together D. Traits are blended Answer: B

What is the classical phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation of Mendel's dihybrid cross (e.g. Yellow Round x Green Wrinkled)? A. 3 : 1 B. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (9 Yellow-Round : 3 Yellow-Wrinkled : 3 Green-Round : 1 Green-Wrinkled) C. 1 : 2 : 1 D. 9 : 7 Answer: B

What is epistasis in genetics? A. One gene has multiple effects B. A phenomenon where the expression of one gene (epistatic gene) masks or suppresses the phenotypic effect of another independent gene (hypostatic gene) C. Gene duplication D. Crossing over Answer: B

What is the modified F2 dihybrid phenotypic ratio in duplicate recessive epistasis (complementary gene action, e.g. Deaf-mutism in humans)? A. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 B. 9 : 7 (presence of dominant alleles of both genes required for normal hearing) C. 13 : 3 D. 15 : 1 Answer: B

What modified F2 dihybrid ratio is produced by dominant epistasis (e.g. White feather color in Leghorn fowls)? A. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 B. 12 : 3 : 1 (or 13 : 3 in dominant and recessive epistasis) C. 9 : 7 D. 15 : 1 Answer: B

What is sex-linked inheritance (discovered by T.H. Morgan in Drosophila fruit flies)? A. Inheritance of autosomes B. Transmission of traits determined by genes carried on the X sex chromosome (X-linked genes) C. Mitochondrial inheritance D. Y-chromosome only Answer: B

Which classic human bleeding disorder is an X-linked recessive genetic trait where blood fails to clot normally (e.g. Royal disease)? A. Sickle cell anemia B. Hemophilia (Hemophilia A: Factor VIII deficiency, Hemophilia B: Factor IX deficiency) C. Thalassemia D. Leukemia Answer: B

Red-green color blindness is an X-linked recessive condition; why are human males far more frequently affected than females? A. Males have two X chromosomes B. Males are hemizygous (XY), possessing only one X chromosome; a single recessive allele results in expression C. Males lack Y chromosome D. Females cannot be carriers Answer: B
What is the genetic chromosomal sex determination system in birds, butterflies, and certain fishes? A. XX - XY system B. ZZ (male) - ZW (female) system C. XO system D. Haplodiploidy Answer: B

Who authored 'On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection' in 1859, proposing the theory of biological evolution? A. Jean-Baptiste Lamarck B. Charles Robert Darwin (along with Alfred Russel Wallace) C. Gregor Mendel D. Hugo de Vries Answer: B

What was the evolutionary hypothesis of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck (1809) concerning evolution? A. Natural selection B. Inheritance of acquired characteristics through use and disuse of organs (Lamarckism) C. Mutation theory D. Genetic drift Answer: B

What are homologous organs in evolutionary comparative anatomy? A. Organs having same function but different structure B. Organs having a common embryonic origin and basic structural plan but modified to perform different functions (e.g. Forelimbs of human, bat, bird, whale) C. Vestigial organs D. Analogous organs Answer: B

What are analogous organs in evolutionary biology? A. Organs with common origin B. Organs performing similar functions and superficial resemblance but having fundamentally different anatomical origin and structure (e.g. Wings of insect and wings of bird - convergent evolution) C. Homologous organs D. Vestigial organs Answer: B

What is taxis?

    Answer: Taxis is directional movement of an organism or cell towards or away from a stimulus.

 What is habituation?

    Answer: Habituation is a simple form of learning in which response to a repeated, harmless stimulus decreases over
    time.
content.long_questions:
Distinguish between innate and learned behaviour with examples.

    Answer: Innate behaviour is largely inherited and can be performed without prior experience, such as a reflex or a
    species-typical courtship pattern. Learned behaviour is modified by experience, such as habituation, conditioning or
    problem-solving. Many behaviours combine inherited tendencies with learning and environmental influence.

mcqs.content: What is the scientific study of animal behavior under natural ecological conditions called? A. Ecology B. Ethology (term coined by Konrad Lorenz, Niko Tinbergen, and Karl von Frisch - Nobel Prize 1973) C. Entomology D. Physiology Answer: B

What is innate (instinctive) behavior in animals? A. Behavior learned by trial and error B. Genetically pre-programmed, stereotypic behavior performed automatically without prior experience or learning C. Conditioned reflex D. Habituation Answer: B

What is a Fixed Action Pattern (FAP) in ethology? A. A voluntary action B. An unlearned, stereotypic, species-specific sequence of innate behavioral acts triggered by an external sign stimulus (releaser) and carried to completion once initiated C. Learned trick D. Random movement Answer: B

In Niko Tinbergen's classic experiment on the male three-spined stickleback fish, what was the sign stimulus triggering territorial attack behavior? A. Size of fish B. Red belly color of the intruder fish (even on crude non-fish models with red undersides) C. Shape of fins D. Water temperature Answer: B

What is taxes (singular: Taxis) in animal orientation behavior? A. Random movement B. A direct, oriented directional locomotor response of an organism toward (positive) or away from (negative) a directional stimulus C. Speed change without direction D. Learning Answer: B
The movement of Euglena or moths directly toward a light source is an example of: A. Negative phototaxis B. Positive Phototaxis C. Chemotaxis D. Geotaxis Answer: B
The movement of a fruit fly (Drosophila) upward against the force of gravity is an example of: A. Positive phototaxis B. Negative Geotaxis (gravitaxis) C. Positive chemotaxis D. Hydrotaxis Answer: B

What is an involuntary, rapid, automated stereotyped response to a sensory stimulus mediated by a reflex arc called? A. Learned habit B. Reflex action (e.g. Knee jerk, blinking, withdrawing hand from hot flame) C. Instinct D. Imprinting Answer: B

What are the essential anatomical components of a simple reflex arc? A. Brain only B. Receptor -> Sensory (afferent) neuron -> Interneuron (CNS) -> Motor (efferent) neuron -> Effector muscle/gland C. Motor neuron to brain D. Sensory cortex only Answer: B

What form of non-associative learning involves a gradual decrease in response to a repeated, benign stimulus that proves neither harmful nor rewarding? A. Classical conditioning B. Habituation (e.g. Scarecrow initially scaring birds, then ignored) C. Sensitization D. Imprinting Answer: B

In Ivan Pavlov's classic conditioning experiments (1904), what was the conditioned stimulus (CS) that elicited salivation in dogs? A. Meat powder (unconditioned stimulus) B. Sound of a bell / metronome (originally neutral, associated with food through repeated pairing) C. Electric shock D. Presence of owner Answer: B

What rapid, irreversible learning occurring during a critical sensitive developmental window was famously demonstrated by Konrad Lorenz with greylag goslings? A. Habituation B. Filial Imprinting (newly hatched goslings follow the first moving object they see) C. Operant conditioning D. Insight learning Answer: B

What complex communicative dance performed by returning forager honeybees (Apis mellifera) communicates the distance and direction of a rich nectar source relative to the Sun? A. Round dance only B. Waggle Dance (figure-eight dance discovered by Karl von Frisch) C. Spiral dance D. Alarm dance Answer: B
What type of dance does a honeybee perform when the food source is close to the hive (less than 50-100 meters away)? A. Waggle dance B. Round dance C. Shake dance D. Tremble dance Answer: B

What chemical messenger substances are secreted externally by animals into the environment to elicit specific behavioral responses in members of the same species? A. Hormones B. Pheromones (e.g., trail, alarm, and sex attractant pheromones like bombykol) C. Neurotransmitters D. Enzymes Answer: B

What is altruistic behavior in sociobiology (e.g. Worker honeybees stinging intruders to defend hive at the cost of their own lives)? A. Selfish behavior B. Self-sacrificing behavior that decreases the individual's direct fitness while increasing the reproductive survival of genetic relatives (Kin Selection) C. Predation D. Territoriality Answer: B
The defense of a defined geographical feeding, mating, or nesting space against conspecific intruders is termed: A. Migration B. Territoriality C. Dispersal D. Dominance hierarchy Answer: B

What is the regular seasonal, cyclical, long-distance round-trip movement of animal populations (e.g. Migratory birds visiting Bangladesh wetlands in winter) called? A. Immigration B. Migration (driven by food availability and breeding conditions) C. Hibernation D. Nomadism Answer: B

What state of dormant inactivity and metabolic depression is entered by certain animals (e.g. Bears, frogs, bats) during cold winter months? A. Aestivation B. Hibernation (winter sleep) C. Torpor only D. Diapause Answer: B

What state of summer dormancy is entered by animals (e.g. Lungfish, snails) to survive high ambient temperatures and drought desiccation? A. Hibernation B. Aestivation (summer sleep) C. Quiescence D. Migration Answer: B
